course: Petrol and Diesel Engine Fundamentals: 0 to 12 Litres

lessons.title: Carburettor Operation and Tuning
lessons.body:
A carburettor mixes petrol and air in the right ratio for your engine. It works on a simple principle: as air rushes through a narrow section called the venturi, it creates a low-pressure area that sucks fuel out of a float chamber. The float chamber keeps a steady level of petrol, like a toilet cistern. The throttle plate controls how much air-fuel mixture enters the engine. When you press the accelerator, the throttle opens, more air flows, and more fuel is drawn in.

In Africa, many older cars, generators, and small engines still use carburettors because they are cheap and easy to fix. Common carburettors include the Weber, Solex, and Mikuni. To tune one, you need a screwdriver, a tachometer (or a good ear), and a warm engine. Start by setting the idle speed screw to about 800-900 RPM for a car, or 2,500-3,000 RPM for a generator. Then adjust the idle mixture screw: turn it in (clockwise) until the engine slows, then out (counter-clockwise) until it runs smoothly. Find the point where the engine runs fastest, then turn the screw in (clockwise) about 1/8 to 1/4 turn to slightly lean the mixture.

Fuel quality matters. In many parts of Africa, petrol can contain dirt or water. Always fit a clear inline fuel filter before the carburettor. Check the float chamber for sediment and clean it with carburettor cleaner. The float height must be set to specâusually 18-22 mm from the carburettor body to the float top when inverted. If the float is too high, fuel overflows; too low, the engine starves.

A common mistake is overtightening the mixture screw, which damages the seat. Turn it gently until it just seats, then back it out 1.5 turns as a starting point. Also, check for vacuum leaks at the intake manifoldâspray WD-40 around the gaskets; if the engine speed changes, you have a leak. Tuning a carburettor is a skill that pays off in rural areas where fuel injection parts are scarce. Practice on a small generator first.

lessons.title: Port Fuel Injection (PFI) Systems
lessons.body:
Port Fuel Injection (PFI) replaced carburettors on most cars from the late 1980s onward. Instead of one central carburettor, PFI has one fuel injector per cylinder, mounted in the intake manifold just before the intake valve. The injector sprays a fine mist of petrol onto the back of the valve. When the valve opens, the air-fuel mixture enters the cylinder. This gives better fuel control, lower emissions, and easier starting.

The main parts are the fuel pump (usually electric, in the tank), fuel filter, fuel rail, pressure regulator, injectors, and the ECU (Engine Control Unit). The pump sends petrol at high pressureâtypically 2.5 to 4.0 bar (36-58 psi)âto the fuel rail. The pressure regulator keeps that pressure steady. The ECU pulses each injector open for a few milliseconds, depending on how much air is entering the engine. More air = longer pulse = more fuel.

In Africa, PFI systems are common on Toyota Corollas, Nissan Sunnys, and many Chinese and Indian cars. A big advantage is that they are less sensitive to altitude and temperature than carburettors. But they need clean fuel. Dirt in the injectors causes misfires, rough idle, and poor fuel economy. Use a good quality fuel filter and replace it every 20,000-30,000 km. If you suspect clogged injectors, you can remove them and send them for ultrasonic cleaningâmany workshops in cities offer this service. Alternatively, use a fuel injector cleaner additive in the tank every 5,000 km.

Diagnosing PFI faults: If the engine cranks but won't start, check for fuel pressure at the rail using a pressure gauge. If pressure is low, suspect the pump, filter, or regulator. If pressure is good, check for injector pulse with a noid light (a cheap LED tool). No pulse means an electrical issueâwiring, ECU, or crank sensor. A common roadside fix is to tap the fuel tank with a rubber mallet to wake up a failing pump, but that's temporary. Always carry a spare fuel filter and a basic multimeter.

lessons.title: Direct Injection (GDI) Systems
lessons.body:
Direct Injection (DI), also called Gasoline Direct Injection (GDI), is the most modern petrol fuel system. Instead of spraying fuel into the intake manifold, the injector sits inside the combustion chamber and sprays petrol directly onto the piston crown. This allows very precise fuel control, higher compression ratios, and better fuel economy. It also lets the engine run in 'lean burn' mode, using less fuel at cruise.

GDI systems operate at much higher fuel pressures: 50 to 200 bar (725-2900 psi). A mechanical high-pressure pump, driven by the camshaft, boosts pressure from the low-pressure in-tank pump. The injectors are solenoid or piezo-electric and fire multiple times per cycle. The ECU uses sensors like the high-pressure fuel sensor, wideband oxygen sensor, and knock sensor to fine-tune injection.

In Africa, GDI is found on newer cars like the Volkswagen Golf TSI, Ford EcoBoost, and many Korean and Chinese models. The main problem with GDI is carbon buildup on the intake valves because no fuel washes them. This causes rough idle, misfires, and power loss. The fix is walnut blastingâa workshop procedure where crushed walnut shells are blown onto the valves to clean them. It costs more than a carburettor tune but is necessary every 60,000-80,000 km.

Another issue is fuel quality. GDI injectors have tiny holes (as small as 0.1 mm) and are easily clogged by dirty petrol. Always use a high-quality fuel filter and change it every 15,000-20,000 km. If you get a check engine light with codes like P0087 (fuel rail pressure too low), suspect the high-pressure pump or a leaking injector. You can check low-pressure side with a gauge (should be 4-6 bar), but high-pressure testing requires a scan tool that reads live data. Do not attempt to open a GDI injectorâit is not serviceable. Replace it as a unit. For rural mechanics, GDI is best left to specialists, but understanding the basics helps you explain the problem to the customer.

lessons.title: Fuel Pumps, Lines, and Filters
lessons.body:
The fuel pump delivers petrol from the tank to the engine. There are two main types: mechanical and electric. Mechanical pumps are found on older carburettor cars; they bolt to the engine block and are driven by a camshaft lobe. They pull fuel from the tank using a diaphragm and check valves. Electric pumps are used on all fuel-injected cars; they sit inside the fuel tank (in-tank pump) and push fuel forward. They are cooled and lubricated by the petrol itself, so never run the tank dryâit can overheat the pump.

Fuel lines carry petrol from the tank to the engine. They are usually steel or plastic. Check for leaks, kinks, and rust. In Africa, poor roads and corrosion can cause lines to rub against the chassis. Use a flashlight and look for wet spots. If you smell petrol, stop the engine immediately. For a temporary repair, you can use a rubber fuel hose and clamps, but replace it with a proper line as soon as possible.

Fuel filters trap dirt, rust, and water. There are two types: inline (plastic or metal canister) and in-tank (a sock on the pump). Replace the inline filter every 20,000-30,000 km, or more often if you buy fuel from jerrycans. A clogged filter causes low fuel pressure, hesitation, and stalling. To test, disconnect the fuel line after the filter and crank the engine; you should get a strong pulse of fuel. If not, replace the filter.

On many African roads, fuel contamination is common. Always carry a spare fuel filter and a filter wrench. When changing the filter, relieve fuel pressure firstâremove the fuel pump fuse and crank the engine for a few seconds. Then disconnect the battery negative. Use a rag to catch spilled petrol. After fitting the new filter, turn the ignition on and off a few times to prime the system, then check for leaks. A simple fuel pressure gauge (0-10 bar) is a worthwhile investment. It costs about $20 and can save hours of guessing.

lessons.title: Electronic Control Unit (ECU) and Sensors
lessons.body:
The Electronic Control Unit (ECU) is the brain of a fuel-injected engine. It reads signals from sensors, decides how much fuel to inject and when to fire the spark, and adjusts idle speed. In Africa, ECUs are common on all cars from the 1990s onward. They are usually located under the dashboard or in the engine bay. They are robust but can fail due to water, heat, or voltage spikes.

The key sensors for fuel systems are: Mass Air Flow (MAF) sensor, Manifold Absolute Pressure (MAP) sensor, Throttle Position Sensor (TPS), Oxygen (O2) sensor, Coolant Temperature Sensor (CTS), and Crankshaft Position (CKP) sensor. The MAF measures how much air enters the engine; it uses a heated wire or film. If it gets dirty, the engine runs lean or rich. You can clean it with MAF cleaner spray (not carb cleaner). The MAP sensor measures vacuum in the intake manifold; it is used on speed-density systems. The TPS tells the ECU how far the accelerator is pressed. The O2 sensor measures oxygen in the exhaust; it fine-tunes fuel mixture. A bad O2 sensor causes poor fuel economy and failed emissions.

The CKP sensor is criticalâit tells the ECU when to fire the injectors and spark. If it fails, the engine won't start. You can test it with a multimeter for resistance (typically 500-1500 ohms) or with an oscilloscope. A common roadside symptom is cranking but no start, with no spark and no injector pulse.

Diagnosing ECU faults: You need an OBD-II scan tool. These cost from $30 for a basic Bluetooth dongle and a phone app. Read the trouble codes. For example, P0100 = MAF circuit malfunction, P0115 = coolant temp sensor, P0335 = crankshaft position sensor. Always check the wiring and connectors firstâcorrosion and loose pins are more common than a dead ECU. If you must replace an ECU, it often needs coding to the car's immobilizer. In rural areas, find a mechanic with a laptop and the right software. Never disconnect the battery while the engine is runningâit can fry the ECU.

lessons.title: Diagnosing Common Fuel System Faults
lessons.body:
Diagnosing fuel system faults starts with listening and asking questions. Does the engine crank but not start? Does it start then die? Does it misfire only when hot? Does it lack power going uphill? Each symptom points to a different part of the system. You need a basic tool kit: a fuel pressure gauge, a noid light, a multimeter, a scan tool, and a spark tester.

First, check the basics. Is there fuel in the tank? Is the fuel filter clogged? On carburettor cars, remove the air cleaner and look down the throat while pumping the acceleratorâyou should see a squirt of petrol. If not, the accelerator pump or float needle is stuck. On fuel-injected cars, connect a fuel pressure gauge to the test port on the fuel rail. Crank the engine. You should see 2.5-4.0 bar for PFI, or 50-200 bar for GDI (use a high-pressure gauge). If pressure is zero, check the fuel pump fuse, relay, and inertia switch (a safety cut-off that trips in a crash).

If pressure is good but the engine won't start, check for spark and injector pulse. Use a noid light on one injector connectorâit should blink while cranking. No blink means the ECU is not firing the injector. Check the CKP sensor and its wiring. If you have spark and pulse, the problem is likely mechanicalâlow compression or a jumped timing belt.

For rough idle or misfire, check for vacuum leaks. Spray carb cleaner around intake gaskets and vacuum hoses; if idle changes, you found the leak. Check the spark plugsâa black, sooty plug means rich mixture; a white, blistered plug means lean. On PFI, a single misfiring cylinder often means a clogged injector. Swap it with another cylinderâif the misfire moves, the injector is bad. On GDI, carbon buildup on intake valves is a common cause; a walnut blast may be needed.

Finally, remember that many 'fuel' problems are actually electrical. A weak battery or bad ground can cause the pump to run slowly. Always check battery voltage (12.6V engine off, 13.5-14.5V running) and clean the terminals. In Africa, dirty fuel is the number one cause of injector failure. Carry spare filters and a can of injector cleaner. If you get a check engine light, read the codes before replacing parts. Guessing wastes money.

quiz.q: What is the main function of the venturi in a carburettor?
options: B) To create a low-pressure area that draws fuel
quiz.explanation: The venturi narrows the air passage, increasing air speed and lowering pressure, which sucks fuel into the airstream.

quiz.q: When tuning a carburettor, what is the typical idle speed for a car engine?
quiz.explanation: Most car engines idle smoothly at 800-900 RPM; generators often idle higher.

quiz.q: What should you do if you suspect a vacuum leak around the intake manifold?
options: B) Spray WD-40 around gaskets and listen for speed change
quiz.explanation: Spraying a flammable liquid around gaskets can temporarily seal a leak and change engine speed, indicating the leak location.

quiz.q: In a Port Fuel Injection (PFI) system, where is the fuel injector mounted?
options: B) In the intake manifold before the intake valve
quiz.explanation: PFI injectors spray fuel onto the back of the intake valve, outside the combustion chamber.

quiz.q: What is the typical fuel pressure for a PFI system?
quiz.explanation: PFI systems operate at relatively low pressure, usually 2.5 to 4.0 bar (36-58 psi).

quiz.q: Which tool is used to check for injector pulse?
quiz.explanation: A noid light plugs into the injector connector and blinks when the ECU fires the injector.

quiz.q: What is a common problem with GDI engines that does not affect PFI engines?
options: B) Carbon buildup on intake valves
quiz.explanation: Because GDI injects fuel directly into the cylinder, no fuel washes the intake valves, leading to carbon deposits.

quiz.q: What is the typical fuel pressure for a GDI system?
quiz.explanation: GDI systems use high-pressure pumps to achieve 50-200 bar for precise injection.

quiz.q: What is 'walnut blasting' used for?
options: B) Removing carbon from intake valves
quiz.explanation: Walnut blasting uses crushed walnut shells to gently remove carbon deposits from GDI intake valves.

quiz.q: Why should you never run a fuel-injected car with a nearly empty tank?
options: A) The fuel pump may overheat
B) The engine will run too rich
C) The spark plugs will foul
quiz.explanation: In-tank electric fuel pumps are cooled and lubricated by petrol; running dry can cause overheating and failure.

quiz.q: How often should you replace an inline fuel filter on a typical PFI car?
quiz.explanation: Most manufacturers recommend replacing the inline fuel filter every 20,000-30,000 km, sooner if fuel quality is poor.

quiz.q: What is the first step before changing a fuel filter on a fuel-injected car?
quiz.explanation: Relieving pressure prevents dangerous fuel spray when disconnecting lines.

quiz.q: Which sensor measures the amount of air entering the engine?
quiz.explanation: The MAF sensor directly measures the mass of air entering the engine, which the ECU uses to calculate fuel delivery.

quiz.q: What does a P0335 trouble code indicate?
quiz.explanation: P0335 is the generic OBD-II code for a crankshaft position sensor 'A' circuit malfunction.

quiz.q: What is the typical resistance range for a crankshaft position sensor?
quiz.explanation: Most inductive crankshaft position sensors have a resistance between 500 and 1500 ohms.

quiz.q: Which of these is a symptom of a clogged fuel filter?
options: B) Hesitation and stalling at high speed
quiz.explanation: A clogged filter restricts fuel flow, causing the engine to hesitate or stall under load.

quiz.q: What should you check first if an engine cranks but won't start?
options: B) Check for fuel pressure and spark
quiz.explanation: The two basic requirements for starting are fuel and spark; checking these first saves time and money.

quiz.q: On a carburettor engine, what does a squirt of fuel from the accelerator pump indicate?
options: B) The accelerator pump is working
C) The idle mixture is too lean
quiz.explanation: When you pump the accelerator, the accelerator pump should inject a visible stream of fuel into the carburettor throat.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the inertia switch in a fuel system?
options: B) To cut off fuel in a crash
quiz.explanation: The inertia switch is a safety device that trips during a collision, shutting off the fuel pump to prevent fire.

quiz.q: Which sensor is used to fine-tune fuel mixture by measuring oxygen in the exhaust?
quiz.explanation: The oxygen sensor provides feedback to the ECU about whether the mixture is rich or lean.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of a single cylinder misfire on a PFI engine?
quiz.explanation: A clogged injector on one cylinder causes that cylinder to run lean or not fire, resulting in a misfire.

quiz.q: How can you test for a vacuum leak?
options: A) Spray carb cleaner around intake gaskets
quiz.explanation: Spraying carb cleaner around suspected leak areas will cause the engine idle to change if a leak is present.

quiz.q: What does a black, sooty spark plug indicate?
quiz.explanation: A black, sooty plug is a sign of too much fuel (rich mixture) or a weak ignition system.

quiz.q: What is the typical battery voltage with the engine running?
quiz.explanation: A healthy charging system should maintain 13.5 to 14.5 volts while the engine is running.

quiz.q: Which fuel system component is cooled and lubricated by petrol?
quiz.explanation: The in-tank electric fuel pump relies on the petrol to cool and lubricate its internal parts.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to check if you smell petrol while driving?
options: B) Stop the engine and check for leaks
quiz.explanation: A petrol smell indicates a dangerous leak; stop the engine immediately and inspect fuel lines and connections.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a sensor used by the ECU for fuel control?
quiz.explanation: The fuel level sensor only operates the fuel gauge; it is not used for engine fuel mixture control.

quiz.q: On a GDI engine, what does a P0087 code indicate?
options: A) Fuel rail pressure too low
quiz.explanation: P0087 is a generic code for 'Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too Low', often caused by a failing high-pressure pump.

quiz.q: What is a safe way to clean a MAF sensor?
quiz.explanation: MAF sensors are delicate; only use a cleaner specifically designed for them to avoid damage.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the fuel pressure regulator in a PFI system?
options: A) To increase fuel pressure with engine speed
B) To maintain constant fuel pressure
quiz.explanation: The regulator keeps fuel pressure steady relative to intake manifold pressure, ensuring consistent injector flow.
